geo-quake-01-c1.text: U.S. Geological Survey, Earthquake Hazards Program (n.d.). The Great 1906 San Francisco Earthquake (excerpted from Ellsworth, 1990). earthquake.usgs.gov.
geo-quake-01-c1.quote: The great earthquake broke loose some 20 to 25 seconds later, with an epicenter near San Francisco. Violent shocks punctuated the strong shaking which lasted some 45 to 60 seconds.
geo-quake-01-c1.claim: Violent shocks punctuated strong shaking that lasted some 45 to 60 seconds.

geo-quake-01-c1.text: U.S. Geological Survey, Earthquake Hazards Program (n.d.). Reid's Elastic Rebound Theory. earthquake.usgs.gov.
geo-quake-01-c1.quote: This picture, taken near Bolinas in Marin County by G.K. Gilbert, shows a fence that was offset about 8.5 feet along the trace of the fault
geo-quake-01-c1.claim: a fence near Bolinas in Marin County that crossed the fault had been cut in two, its halves offset by about 8.5 feet (2.6 meters).

geo-quake-01-c1.text: Thatcher, W., Marshall, G., & Lisowski, M. (1997). Resolution of fault slip along the 470-km-long rupture of the great 1906 San Francisco earthquake and its implications. Journal of Geophysical Research: Solid Earth 102(B3), 5353-5367.
geo-quake-01-c1.quote: Slip decreases from maxima of 8.6 and 7.5 m at Shelter Cove and Tomales Bay to 4.5 m near Mount Tamalpais and 2.7 m at Loma Prieta.
geo-quake-01-c1.claim: resurveys of the ground put the slip at up to 7.5 meters at Tomales Bay and 8.6 meters at Shelter Cove.

geo-quake-01-c1.text: U.S. Geological Survey, Earthquake Hazards Program (n.d.). 1906 Marked the Dawn of the Scientific Revolution. earthquake.usgs.gov.
geo-quake-01-c1.quote: it was found after 1906 that displacements in the earthquake were largest at the fault and decreased with distance from it, so that a previously straight line crossing the fault had become curved.
geo-quake-01-c1.claim: the ground had moved most right beside the fault, and less and less with distance from it, so a line that had been straight across the fault was now curved.

geo-quake-01-c1.text: U.S. Geological Survey, Earthquake Hazards Program (n.d.). Reid's Elastic Rebound Theory. earthquake.usgs.gov.
geo-quake-01-c1.quote: Henry Fielding Reid, Professor of Geology at Johns Hopkins University, concluded that the earthquake must have involved an "elastic rebound" of previously stored elastic stress.
geo-quake-01-c1.claim: Reid concluded that the earthquake was an elastic rebound: the crust had slowly stored elastic strain, then released it all at once.

geo-quake-01-c1.text: U.S. Geological Survey, Earthquake Hazards Program (n.d.). Reid's Elastic Rebound Theory. earthquake.usgs.gov.
geo-quake-01-c1.quote: As the Pacific plate moves northwest, it gradually distorts the fence. Just before an earthquake, the fence has an "S" shape. When the earthquake occurs the distortion is released and the two parts of the fence are again straight; but now there is an offset.
geo-quake-01-c1.claim: When the fault slips, the bend springs back and both halves are straight again, but now they are offset.

geo-quake-01-c1.text: U.S. Geological Survey, Earthquake Hazards Program (n.d.). 1906 Marked the Dawn of the Scientific Revolution. earthquake.usgs.gov.
geo-quake-01-c1.quote: this basic mechanical concept of earthquakes -- that the faulting causes the earthquake and that the earthquake does not cause the faulting -- was not well recognized as a universal principle
geo-quake-01-c1.claim: Reid's idea turned the old order around: the faulting causes the earthquake, not the other way round.

geo-quake-01-c1.text: U.S. Geological Survey, Earthquake Hazards Program (n.d.). When will it happen again? (1906 San Francisco earthquake). earthquake.usgs.gov.
geo-quake-01-c1.quote: Based on models taking into account the long-term rate of slip on the San Andreas fault and the amount of offset that occurred on the fault in 1906, the best guess is that 1906-type earthquakes occur at intervals of about 200 years.
geo-quake-01-c1.claim: 1906-sized earthquakes on this part of the San Andreas come about every 200 years

geo-quake-01-c2.text: Ishii, M., Shearer, P. M., Houston, H., & Vidale, J. E. (2005). Extent, duration and speed of the 2004 Sumatra-Andaman earthquake imaged by the Hi-Net array. Nature 435, 933-936.
geo-quake-01-c2.quote: We used the Hi-Net seismic array in Japan as an antenna to map the progression of slip by monitoring the direction of high-frequency radiation. We find that the rupture spread over the entire 1,300-km-long aftershock zone by propagating northward at roughly 2.8 km s-1 for approximately 8 minutes.
geo-quake-01-c2.claim: seismologists tracked the rupture as it ran north: about 1,300 kilometers in roughly 8 minutes, at about 2.8 kilometers per second.

geo-quake-01-c2.text: Ishii, M., Shearer, P. M., Houston, H., & Vidale, J. E. (2005). Extent, duration and speed of the 2004 Sumatra-Andaman earthquake imaged by the Hi-Net array. Nature 435, 933-936.
geo-quake-01-c2.quote: Its rupture, in both duration and extent, is the longest ever recorded.
geo-quake-01-c2.claim: In both duration and extent, it was the longest rupture ever recorded.

geo-quake-01-c2.text: Burkett, E. R., Given, D. D., & Jones, L. M. (2014, revised 2017). ShakeAlert: An earthquake early warning system for the United States west coast. U.S. Geological Survey Fact Sheet 2014-3083.
geo-quake-01-c2.quote: The rupture begins at one point on the fault and rapidly extends along some distance of the fault, like a lengthening crack in a car windshield. As the rupture travels along the fault, the sudden movement of the two sides of the fault generates seismic (shaking) waves that radiate outward through the Earth
geo-quake-01-c2.claim: spreads along the fault like a lengthening crack in a car windshield

geo-quake-01-c2.text: U.S. Geological Survey, Earthquake Hazards Program (n.d.). How long was the 1906 rupture? earthquake.usgs.gov.
geo-quake-01-c2.quote: The total length is 296 miles (477 kilometers). For comparison, the 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake had a rupture length of about 25 miles (40 km).
geo-quake-01-c2.claim: The 1906 San Francisco rupture was 477 kilometers long; the 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake broke about 40.

geo-quake-01-c2.text: U.S. Geological Survey (n.d.). Earthquakes (General Interest Publication): How Earthquakes Happen. pubs.usgs.gov.
geo-quake-01-c2.quote: Normal faults occur in response to pulling or tension; the overlying block moves down the dip of the fault plane. Thrust (reverse) faults occur in response to squeezing or compression; the overlying block moves up the dip of the fault plane. Strike-slip (lateral) faults occur in response to either type of stress; the blocks move horizontally past one another.
geo-quake-01-c2.claim: geologists sort faults into three main groups

geo-quake-01-c2.text: U.S. Geological Survey (n.d.). Earthquakes (General Interest Publication): How Earthquakes Happen. pubs.usgs.gov.
geo-quake-01-c2.quote: Most faulting along spreading zones is normal, along subduction zones is thrust, and along transform faults is strike-slip.
geo-quake-01-c2.claim: Spreading zones mostly have normal faults, subduction zones thrust faults, and transform faults strike-slip.

geo-quake-01-c2.text: U.S. Geological Survey, Earthquake Hazards Program (n.d.). The Great 1906 San Francisco Earthquake (excerpted from Ellsworth, 1990). earthquake.usgs.gov.
geo-quake-01-c2.quote: the earthquake confounded contemporary geologists with its large, horizontal displacements and great rupture length.
geo-quake-01-c2.claim: The 1906 earthquake, which baffled geologists of the day with its large horizontal displacements

geo-quake-01-c3.text: U.S. Geological Survey, Earthquake Hazards Program (n.d.). Aftershock Forecast Overview. earthquake.usgs.gov.
geo-quake-01-c3.quote: For example, the 2011 M9.1 Japan earthquake and tsunami was preceded by a M7.3 foreshock two days before. When the M7.3 earthquake first occurred, it was called the mainshock, and then when the M9.1 earthquake occurred, that larger earthquake became the mainshock.
geo-quake-01-c3.claim: In 2011 a magnitude 7.3 earthquake struck Japan, and for two days it was the mainshock.

geo-quake-01-c3.text: U.S. Geological Survey, Earthquake Hazards Program (n.d.). Aftershock Forecast Overview. earthquake.usgs.gov.
geo-quake-01-c3.quote: A small fraction of earthquakes are followed by a larger earthquake, in which case the first earthquake is referred to as a foreshock.
geo-quake-01-c3.claim: The label comes only in hindsight, if something bigger follows, and only a small fraction of earthquakes are followed by a larger one.

geo-quake-01-c3.text: Guglielmi, A., Klain, B., Zavyalov, A., & Zotov, O. (2023). Omori Law. To the 100th anniversary of death of the famous Japanese seismologist. arXiv:2302.01277.
geo-quake-01-c3.quote: In 1894 he formulated the law of aftershock evolution. Omori's Law states that after the main shock of an earthquake, the frequency of aftershocks decreases hyperbolically with time.
geo-quake-01-c3.claim: In 1894 the Japanese seismologist Fusakichi Omori formulated their law: after the main shock, the frequency of aftershocks decreases hyperbolically with time.

geo-quake-01-c3.text: U.S. Geological Survey, Earthquake Hazards Program (n.d.). Aftershock Forecast Overview. earthquake.usgs.gov.
geo-quake-01-c3.quote: The rate of aftershocks decreases with time, such that the earthquake rate is roughly inversely proportional to the time since the mainshock. In other words, there are about 10 times as many aftershocks on the first day as on the tenth day.
geo-quake-01-c3.claim: the rate is roughly inversely proportional to the time since the mainshock, so there are about 10 times as many aftershocks on the first day as on the tenth.

geo-quake-01-c3.text: Utsu, T., Ogata, Y., & Matsu'ura, R. S. (1995). The Centenary of the Omori Formula for a Decay Law of Aftershock Activity. Journal of Physics of the Earth 43(1), 1-33.
geo-quake-01-c3.quote: Studies published during the last 1/3 century confirmed that the modified Omori formula generally provides an appropriate representation of the temporal variation of aftershock activity.
geo-quake-01-c3.claim: A century on, studies were still finding that a modified form of Omori's formula describes aftershock decay well.

geo-quake-01-c3.text: U.S. Geological Survey, Earthquake Hazards Program (n.d.). Aftershock Forecast Overview. earthquake.usgs.gov.
geo-quake-01-c3.quote: The magnitudes of the aftershocks don't change with time, meaning that large aftershocks are still possible later in the sequence, as happened following Northridge.
geo-quake-01-c3.claim: Aftershock magnitudes don't shrink with time, so a large aftershock can still strike late in a sequence.

geo-quake-01-c3.text: Shearer, P. M. (2012). Self-similar earthquake triggering, Båth's law, and foreshock/aftershock magnitudes: Simulations, theory, and results for southern California. Journal of Geophysical Research 117(B6). Abstract via Statewide California Earthquake Center.
geo-quake-01-c3.quote: Båth’s law, the observation that the largest aftershock is, on average, 1.2 magnitudes smaller than its main shock, independent of main shock size
geo-quake-01-c3.claim: on average the largest aftershock is about 1.2 magnitudes smaller than its mainshock, whatever the mainshock's size.

geo-quake-01-c3.text: U.S. Geological Survey, Earthquake Hazards Program (n.d.). Aftershock Forecast Overview. earthquake.usgs.gov.
geo-quake-01-c3.quote: Following a significant earthquake, this aftershock forecast can provide situational awareness of the expected number of aftershocks, as well as the probability of subsequent larger earthquakes.
geo-quake-01-c3.claim: USGS aftershock forecasts are given as probabilities, including the probability of a later, larger earthquake.

geo-quake-02-c1.text: U.S. Geological Survey (n.d.). Earthquakes (General Interest Publication): Measuring Earthquakes. pubs.usgs.gov.
geo-quake-02-c1.quote: The first indication of an earthquake is often a sharp thud, signaling the arrival of compressional waves. This is followed by the shear waves and then the "ground roll" caused by the surface waves.
geo-quake-02-c1.claim: The first sign is often a sharp thud as the compressional waves hit, then come the shear waves, and last the rolling "ground roll" of the surface waves.

geo-quake-02-c1.text: Britannica Editors (2026). Seismic wave. Encyclopaedia Britannica.
geo-quake-02-c1.quote: In the Earth, P waves travel at speeds from about 6 km (3.7 miles) per second in surface rock to about 10.4 km (6.5 miles) per second near the Earth’s core
geo-quake-02-c1.claim: are the fastest, at about 6 kilometers per second in surface rock.

geo-quake-02-c1.text: UPSeis, Michigan Technological University (n.d.). Body Waves. mtu.edu.
geo-quake-02-c1.quote: P waves can move through solid rock and fluids, like water or the liquid layers of the Earth. It squishes and stretches the rock it moves through just like sound waves compress and expand the air as they move through it.
geo-quake-02-c1.claim: They squeeze and stretch the rock in the direction they travel, the way sound compresses and expands air, and they cross fluids such as water as well as solid rock.

geo-quake-02-c1.text: U.S. Geological Survey (n.d.). Earthquakes (General Interest Publication): How Earthquakes Happen. pubs.usgs.gov.
geo-quake-02-c1.quote: Some of the vibrations are of high enough frequency to be audible, while others are of very low frequency.
geo-quake-02-c1.claim: Some of the vibrations are high enough in frequency to be heard.

geo-quake-02-c1.text: UPSeis, Michigan Technological University (n.d.). Body Waves. mtu.edu.
geo-quake-02-c1.quote: An S wave is about 1.7 times slower than a P wave. The biggest difference is that S waves can’t move through liquids. Because S waves only move through solids, seismologists were led to conclude that the Earth's outer core is a liquid.
geo-quake-02-c1.claim: They are about 1.7 times slower than P waves and cannot cross liquids, which is how they gave away Earth's liquid outer core.

geo-quake-02-c1.text: Britannica Editors (2026). Seismic wave. Encyclopaedia Britannica.
geo-quake-02-c1.quote: In the Earth the speed of S waves increases from about 3.4 km (2.1 miles) per second at the surface
geo-quake-02-c1.claim: Near the surface they move at about 3.4 kilometers per second.

geo-quake-02-c1.text: U.S. Geological Survey (n.d.). Earthquakes (General Interest Publication): Measuring Earthquakes. pubs.usgs.gov.
geo-quake-02-c1.quote: The two general types of vibrations produced by earthquakes are surface waves, which travel along the Earth's surface, and body waves, which travel through the Earth. Surface waves usually have the strongest vibrations and probably cause most of the damage done by earthquakes.
geo-quake-02-c1.claim: they usually carry the strongest vibrations and probably cause most of the damage done by earthquakes.

geo-quake-02-c1.text: UPSeis, Michigan Technological University (n.d.). Surface Waves. mtu.edu.
geo-quake-02-c1.quote: Love waves produce entirely horizontal motion.
geo-quake-02-c1.claim: Love waves shake the ground entirely from side to side.

geo-quake-02-c1.text: UPSeis, Michigan Technological University (n.d.). Surface Waves. mtu.edu.
geo-quake-02-c1.quote: Because it rolls, it moves the ground up and down, and forward and backward in the direction that the wave is moving. Most of the shaking felt from an earthquake is due to the Rayleigh wave, which can be much larger than the other waves.
geo-quake-02-c1.claim: Rayleigh waves roll it, up and down and forward and back, and most of the shaking people feel in an earthquake comes from them.

geo-quake-02-c2.text: Science Museum Group (n.d.). Model of the Zhang Heng seismoscope (object 1976-107). Science Museum Group Collection.
geo-quake-02-c2.quote: The Chinese astronomer, mathematician and seismologist, Zhang Heng (78-139 AD) described the earliest seismoscope known in about 132 AD.
geo-quake-02-c2.claim: In about 132 CE the Chinese astronomer and mathematician Zhang Heng described an instrument for sensing earthquakes, the earliest seismoscope known.

geo-quake-02-c2.text: National Museum of American History, Smithsonian Institution (n.d.). Chinese Seismoscope (replica). americanhistory.si.edu.
geo-quake-02-c2.quote: Zhang’s original instrument was large (perhaps 2 meters in diameter), and complex (with eight dragons at top, each with a frog below). When a seism occurred, a small ball would drop from the mouth of one of the dragons into the open mouth of the corresponding frog.
geo-quake-02-c2.claim: It was a large bronze vessel, perhaps 2 meters across, with eight dragons around the top and a frog beneath each one.

geo-quake-02-c2.text: Encyclopedia of World Biography (n.d.). Heng, Chang. Via Encyclopedia.com.
geo-quake-02-c2.quote: Although Heng's original seismograph did not survive time, its description did, and several modern scholars have tried to recreate the device.
geo-quake-02-c2.claim: The original is lost; only its description survived, and modern scholars have tried to rebuild it from that.

geo-quake-02-c2.text: Lienhard, J. H. (n.d.). No. 324: Chinese Seismology. The Engines of Our Ingenuity, University of Houston.
geo-quake-02-c2.quote: Members of the court thought the device had failed when the alarm sounded one day and they felt nothing. Doubt turned to astonishment a few days later. A messenger arrived from a town 400 miles away to report that it'd been savaged by an earthquake.
geo-quake-02-c2.claim: Days later a messenger arrived from a town about 400 miles (640 km) away with news of an earthquake.

geo-quake-02-c2.text: Feng, R., & Yu, Y. (2006). ZHANG Heng's Seismometer and Longxi earthquake in AD 134. Acta Seismologica Sinica 19, 704-719.
geo-quake-02-c2.quote: Longxi earthquake was the only earthquake example, which ZHANG Heng’s Seismometer had detected.
geo-quake-02-c2.claim: That Longxi earthquake is the only one the seismoscope is known to have detected.

geo-quake-02-c2.text: Feng, R., & Yu, Y. (2006). ZHANG Heng's Seismometer and Longxi earthquake in AD 134. Acta Seismologica Sinica 19, 704-719.
geo-quake-02-c2.quote: especially by analyzing the description of Longxi earthquake of Houhan Shu, by studying the historical background exposed by historical literatures at that time, ZHANG Heng’s biography, his poems and place names of Han Dynasty, by comparing five earthquakes occurred in Qing Dynasty and their attenuation of seismic intensity, the conclusion can be drawn that the Longxi earthquake should take place on December 13, AD 134 (the third year of Yangjia reign). As a rough assessment, the epicenter was in Tianshui area and the magnitude was about 7.
geo-quake-02-c2.claim: dates it to December 13, 134 CE, rather than the often-cited 138, and puts it at about magnitude 7.

geo-quake-02-c2.text: Seismology Research Centre (2022, June 27). Locating the Origin of an Earthquake. src.com.au.
geo-quake-02-c2.quote: Similarly, you can roughly tell how far an earthquake is away by counting the number of seconds between the initial P-wave shake and the stronger S-wave shaking. Because earthquake energy waves travel much faster through rock than sound waves travel through air, the number of seconds between the P and S multiplied by 8 gives you the distance to the earthquake’s origin in kilometres. This is a very rough estimate
geo-quake-02-c2.claim: Multiply the S-minus-P time in seconds by 8 and you get a very rough distance in kilometers.

geo-quake-02-c2.text: UPSeis, Michigan Technological University (n.d.). How Can I Locate the Earthquake Epicenter? mtu.edu.
geo-quake-02-c2.quote: In this case, the first P and S waves are 24 seconds apart. Find the point for 24 seconds on the left side of the chart of simplified S and P travel time curves and mark that point. According to the chart, this earthquake's epicenter was 215 kilometers away.
geo-quake-02-c2.claim: In one worked example, P and S arrive 24 seconds apart, and travel-time curves put the quake 215 kilometers away.

geo-quake-02-c2.text: UPSeis, Michigan Technological University (n.d.). How Can I Locate the Earthquake Epicenter? mtu.edu.
geo-quake-02-c2.quote: The point where the three circles intersect is the epicenter of the earthquake. This technique is called "trilateration."
geo-quake-02-c2.claim: Circles drawn around three stations meet at a single point, the epicenter, a method called trilateration.

geo-quake-02-c3.text: Japan Meteorological Agency (n.d.). Earthquake Early Warning System. jma.go.jp.
geo-quake-02-c3.quote: On 1 October 2007, JMA launched the Earthquake Early Warning service for provision through a number of media outlets such as TV and radio.
geo-quake-02-c3.claim: On October 1, 2007, the Japan Meteorological Agency began sending Earthquake Early Warnings to the public through TV, radio and other media.

geo-quake-02-c3.text: Burkett, E. R., Given, D. D., & Jones, L. M. (2014, revised 2017). ShakeAlert: An earthquake early warning system for the United States west coast. U.S. Geological Survey Fact Sheet 2014-3083.
geo-quake-02-c3.quote: Early warning is possible because information can be sent through communication systems virtually instantaneously, whereas seismic waves travel through the shallow Earth at speeds ranging from 0.5 to 3 miles per second.
geo-quake-02-c3.claim: Seismic waves travel through the shallow Earth at 0.5 to 3 miles (roughly 1 to 5 kilometers) per second, while an alert crosses communication networks almost instantly.

geo-quake-02-c3.text: Burkett, E. R., Given, D. D., & Jones, L. M. (2014, revised 2017). ShakeAlert: An earthquake early warning system for the United States west coast. U.S. Geological Survey Fact Sheet 2014-3083.
geo-quake-02-c3.quote: The faster but weaker P waves trip nearby sensors, causing alert signals to be sent out, giving people and automated electronic systems some time (seconds to minutes) to take protective actions before the arrival of the slower but stronger S waves and surface waves.
geo-quake-02-c3.claim: Sensors near the epicenter pick up the fast but weak P waves, the alert goes out, and people and machines get seconds to act before the slower, stronger S and surface waves arrive.

geo-quake-02-c3.text: Burkett, E. R., Given, D. D., & Jones, L. M. (2014, revised 2017). ShakeAlert: An earthquake early warning system for the United States west coast. U.S. Geological Survey Fact Sheet 2014-3083.
geo-quake-02-c3.quote: The farther a location is from the epicenter, the greater the amount of warning time.
geo-quake-02-c3.claim: The farther you are from the epicenter, the more warning you get.

geo-quake-02-c3.text: Given, D. D., & West Coast ShakeAlert Project Team (2021). ShakeAlert earthquake warning: The challenge of transforming ground motion into protective actions. Proceedings of SMIP 2021 Seminar on Utilization of Strong-Motion Data, 70-76.
geo-quake-02-c3.quote: State-wide public alerting began in California in October of 2019, expanded to Oregon in March of 2021, and to Washington in May of 2021.
geo-quake-02-c3.claim: Statewide public alerts began in California in October 2019, then expanded to Oregon in March 2021 and Washington in May 2021.

geo-quake-02-c3.text: Japan Meteorological Agency (2007, August 30). What is an Earthquake Early Warning? jma.go.jp.
geo-quake-02-c3.quote: The Earthquake Early Warning is aimed at mitigating earthquake-related damage by allowing countermeasures such as promptly slowing down trains, controlling elevators to avoid danger and enabling people to quickly protect themselves
geo-quake-02-c3.claim: Trains can be slowed and elevators controlled before the shaking starts.

geo-quake-02-c3.text: Burkett, E. R., Given, D. D., & Jones, L. M. (2014, revised 2017). ShakeAlert: An earthquake early warning system for the United States west coast. U.S. Geological Survey Fact Sheet 2014-3083.
geo-quake-02-c3.quote: Surgeons, dentists, and others stop delicate procedures.
geo-quake-02-c3.claim: Surgeons and dentists can stop delicate procedures.

geo-quake-02-c3.text: Kuyuk, H. S., & Allen, R. M. (2013). Optimal Seismic Network Density for Earthquake Early Warning: A Case Study from California. Seismological Research Letters 84(6), 946-954.
geo-quake-02-c3.quote: One of the challenges with EEWS is minimizing the blind zone, that is, the region around the epicenter where no warning is possible because the strong shaking has already occurred by the time the alert is generated. Some factors that influence the radius of the blind-zone area are simply out of our control. For example, we cannot dictate exactly where earthquakes occur and how deep an earthquake hypocenter is. However, there are many things we can do to reduce the size of the blind zone.
geo-quake-02-c3.claim: the region around the epicenter where no warning is possible because the strong shaking has already arrived by the time the alert is generated.

geo-quake-02-c3.text: Lux, A. I., Smith, D., Böse, M., McGuire, J. J., Saunders, J. K., et al. (2024). Status and Performance of the ShakeAlert Earthquake Early Warning System: 2019-2023. Bulletin of the Seismological Society of America.
geo-quake-02-c3.quote: Because it takes time to detect earthquakes and distribute the alerts, there will always be a late-alert zone near the epicenter for which no warning is possible.
geo-quake-02-c3.claim: detecting a quake and sending the alert both take time, so there will always be a late-alert zone near the epicenter.

geo-quake-02-c3.text: Japan Meteorological Agency (2007, August 30). Limitations of the Earthquake Early Warning. jma.go.jp.
geo-quake-02-c3.quote: The window of time from the announcement of an Earthquake Early Warning until the arrival of the main tremors is very short, i.e. a matter of seconds (or between several seconds and a few tens of seconds).
geo-quake-02-c3.claim: the gap between alert and strong tremors is a matter of seconds, between several seconds and a few tens of seconds.

geo-quake-03-c1.text: U.S. Geological Survey (n.d.). DYFI Scientific Background. USGS Earthquake Hazards Program.
geo-quake-03-c1.quote: For example, the magnitude of the 1994 Northridge earthquake was 6.7. The intensities ranged from IX (violent) close to the epicenter, to V (moderate) at distances of about 60 - 200 miles away, and finally intensity I (not felt) at even greater distances.
geo-quake-03-c1.claim: The 1994 Northridge earthquake in Los Angeles had one magnitude, 6.7, but the shaking it caused had many values: intensity IX (violent) near the epicenter, V (moderate) about 60 to 200 miles away, and I (not felt) farther out.

geo-quake-03-c1.text: Rafferty, J. P., & Britannica Editors (n.d.). Richter scale. Encyclopaedia Britannica.
geo-quake-03-c1.quote: Richter scale (ML), quantitative measure of an earthquake’s magnitude (size), devised in 1935 by American seismologists Charles F. Richter and Beno Gutenberg.
geo-quake-03-c1.claim: Magnitude measures the quake itself. The first magnitude scale was devised in 1935 by the American seismologists Charles Richter and Beno Gutenberg.

geo-quake-03-c1.text: Richter, C. F. (1935). An instrumental earthquake magnitude scale. Bulletin of the Seismological Society of America, 25(1), 1-32.
geo-quake-03-c1.quote: suggestion of Mr. H. O. Wood, it is here proposed to refer to such a scale as a "magnitude" scale. This terminology is offered in distinction
geo-quake-03-c1.claim: The name was Harry Wood's suggestion, chosen to keep the new instrumental scale apart from the intensity scales already in use.

geo-quake-03-c1.text: U.S. Geological Survey (n.d.). Earthquake Magnitude, Energy Release, and Shaking Intensity. USGS Earthquake Hazards Program.
geo-quake-03-c1.quote: His original definition held only for California earthquakes occurring within 600 km of a particular type of seismograph (the Woods-Anderson torsion instrument).
geo-quake-03-c1.claim: It worked only for California quakes within 600 km of one kind of instrument, the Wood-Anderson torsion seismograph.

geo-quake-03-c1.text: Rafferty, J. P., & Britannica Editors (n.d.). Richter scale. Encyclopaedia Britannica.
geo-quake-03-c1.quote: Since modern seismographs can detect seismic waves even smaller than those originally chosen for zero magnitude, it is possible to measure earthquakes having negative magnitudes on the Richter scale.
geo-quake-03-c1.claim: Zero did not mean no earthquake. It sat near the smallest shocks the seismographs of the 1930s could detect, and today's more sensitive instruments record quakes with negative magnitudes.

geo-quake-03-c1.text: U.S. Geological Survey (n.d.). The Modified Mercalli Intensity Scale. USGS Earthquake Hazards Program.
geo-quake-03-c1.quote: It was developed in 1931 by the American seismologists Harry Wood and Frank Neumann. This scale, composed of increasing levels of intensity that range from imperceptible shaking to catastrophic destruction, is designated by Roman numerals. It does not have a mathematical basis; instead it is an arbitrary ranking based on observed effects.
geo-quake-03-c1.claim: Intensity describes what the shaking did at one spot, from people waking up to furniture moving to damaged chimneys. The scale used in the United States, the Modified Mercalli, was drawn up in 1931 by the same Harry Wood, with Frank Neumann. It runs in Roman numerals from imperceptible shaking to catastrophic destruction, and it has no mathematical basis: it is a ranking of observed effects.

geo-quake-03-c1.text: U.S. Geological Survey (n.d.). DYFI Scientific Background. USGS Earthquake Hazards Program.
geo-quake-03-c1.quote: We group all the responses for an earthquake into “communities” which we define to be ZIP code regions, cities, or rectangular boxes defined by UTM boundaries (see data aggregation). We aggregate all the responses of users in each community and assign a single intensity, called “Community Decimal Intensity” (CDI), to that community.
geo-quake-03-c1.claim: Today the public does much of the observing. The USGS Did You Feel It? survey groups the answers people send in by ZIP code or city and gives each place a single intensity.

geo-quake-03-c1.text: U.S. Geological Survey (n.d.). DYFI Scientific Background. USGS Earthquake Hazards Program.
geo-quake-03-c1.quote: Even if you did not feel the earthquake, your response is important: in areas of lighter shaking, the "not-felt" responses are needed to determine the percentage of felt responses as well as determine the boundary of “felt” and “not felt” areas.
geo-quake-03-c1.claim: Even a reply of "not felt" counts, because it helps mark the edge of the area where the quake was felt.

geo-quake-03-c2.text: Ozaki, T. (2011). Outline of the 2011 off the Pacific coast of Tohoku Earthquake (Mw 9.0): Tsunami warnings/advisories and observations. Earth, Planets and Space, 63, 827-830.
geo-quake-03-c2.quote: JMA issued tsunami warnings/advisories for the destructive tsunami for coasts ranging from Hokkaido to Kyushu, and the Ogasawara islands, within about three minutes after the earthquake. The initial warning issued at 14:49 on March 11 was based on the promptly-estimated JMA Magnitude of 7.9
geo-quake-03-c2.claim: About three minutes after the Tōhoku earthquake struck on March 11, 2011, the Japan Meteorological Agency issued its first tsunami warning, based on a quick magnitude of 7.9.

geo-quake-03-c2.text: Ozaki, T. (2011). Outline of the 2011 off the Pacific coast of Tohoku Earthquake (Mw 9.0): Tsunami warnings/advisories and observations. Earth, Planets and Space, 63, 827-830.
geo-quake-03-c2.quote: It can be calculated within several minutes, but it has a downside to be saturated for a magnitude substantially larger than 8. JMA updated Mjma to 8.4 at 16:00 and determined the moment magnitude (Mw) as 8.8 by CMT analysis at 17:30, which was calculated from overseas broadband seismic data. On March 13, Mw was revised to be 9.0
geo-quake-03-c2.claim: That fast method saturates for quakes much larger than magnitude 8. The agency raised its figure to 8.4 at 4 pm, computed a moment magnitude of 8.8 at 5:30 pm, and on March 13 revised it to 9.0.

geo-quake-03-c2.text: Kanamori, H. (1977). The energy release in great earthquakes. Journal of Geophysical Research, 82(20), 2981-2987.
geo-quake-03-c2.quote: The conventional magnitude scale M suffers saturation when the rupture dimension of the earthquake exceeds the wavelength of the seismic waves used for the magnitude determination (usually 5–50 km). This saturation leads to an inaccurate estimate of energy released in great earthquakes.
geo-quake-03-c2.claim: Saturation is why the older scales fail on giants. They read the height of one kind of seismic wave, and once a rupture grows longer than those waves (usually 5 to 50 km), a bigger break no longer makes a proportionally bigger wave, as Hiroo Kanamori showed in 1977.

geo-quake-03-c2.text: Rafferty, J. P., & Britannica Editors (n.d.). Richter scale. Encyclopaedia Britannica.
geo-quake-03-c2.quote: In theory, the Richter scale has no upper limit, but, in practice, no earthquake has ever been registered on the scale above magnitude 8.6. (That was the Richter magnitude for the Chile earthquake of 1960. The moment magnitude for this event was measured at 9.5.)
geo-quake-03-c2.claim: On the Richter scale, no earthquake has ever registered above 8.6: that was the 1960 Chile earthquake, whose moment magnitude is 9.5.

geo-quake-03-c2.text: U.S. Geological Survey (n.d.). Earthquake Magnitude, Energy Release, and Shaking Intensity. USGS Earthquake Hazards Program.
geo-quake-03-c2.quote: Moment (MO) = rigidity x area x slip where rigidity is the strength of the rock along the fault, area is the area of the fault that slipped, and slip is the distance the fault moved.
geo-quake-03-c2.claim: The cure was to measure the break itself. Seismic moment is rigidity × area × slip: how strong the rock along the fault is, how much fault surface slipped, and how far it moved.

geo-quake-03-c2.text: Hanks, T. C., & Kanamori, H. (1979). A moment magnitude scale. Journal of Geophysical Research, 84(B5), 2348-2350.
geo-quake-03-c2.quote: The nearly coincident forms of the relations between seismic moment M_0 and the magnitudes M_L, M_S, and M_w imply a moment magnitude scale M = ⅔ log M_0 - 10.7 which is uniformly valid for 3 ≲ M_L ≲ 7, 5 ≲ M_s ≲ 7½, and M_w ≳ 7½.
geo-quake-03-c2.claim: In 1979 Tom Hanks and Kanamori turned moment into the moment magnitude scale, Mw, built to agree with the older scales where they work and to keep counting where they stop.

geo-quake-03-c2.text: U.S. Geological Survey (n.d.). Earthquake Magnitude, Energy Release, and Shaking Intensity. USGS Earthquake Hazards Program.
geo-quake-03-c2.quote: If the San Andreas Fault were to rupture end-to-end (~1400km), with ~10m of average slip, it would produce an earthquake of Mw 8.47. If the South American subduction zone were to rupture end-to-end (~6400km), with ~40m of average slip, it would produce an earthquake of Mw 9.86.
geo-quake-03-c2.claim: Because moment grows with fault area, the size of a fault caps the size of its quakes. If the whole San Andreas Fault, about 1,400 km long, slipped 10 m at once, USGS calculates it would make a magnitude 8.47; the South American subduction zone, about 6,400 km long and slipping 40 m, would make a 9.86.

geo-quake-03-c2.text: U.S. Geological Survey (n.d.). Earthquake Magnitude, Energy Release, and Shaking Intensity. USGS Earthquake Hazards Program.
geo-quake-03-c2.quote: You would need ~14,000km fault length, with a seismogenic thickness averaging 40km (width of 100km), to slip and average of 30m to produce an Mw 10.
geo-quake-03-c2.claim: A magnitude 10 would need a fault about 14,000 km long, over a third of the way around the planet, slipping 30 m.

geo-quake-03-c3.text: U.S. Geological Survey (n.d.). M 9.5 - 1960 Great Chilean Earthquake (Valdivia Earthquake). ANSS Comprehensive Earthquake Catalog event page.
geo-quake-03-c3.claim: The top of the list belongs to the Valdivia earthquake in southern Chile: magnitude 9.5, on May 22, 1960.

geo-quake-03-c3.text: Brocher, T. M., Filson, J. R., Fuis, G. S., Haeussler, P. J., Holzer, T. L., Plafker, G., & Blair, J. L. (2014). The 1964 Great Alaska Earthquake and Tsunamis: A Modern Perspective and Enduring Legacies. USGS Fact Sheet 2014-3018.
geo-quake-03-c3.quote: The magnitude 9.2 Great Alaska Earthquake that struck south-central Alaska at 5:36 p.m. on Friday, March 27, 1964, is the largest recorded earthquake in U.S. history and the second-largest earthquake recorded with modern instruments. The earthquake was felt throughout most of mainland Alaska, as far west as Dutch Harbor in the Aleutian Islands some 480 miles away, and at Seattle, Washington, more than 1,200 miles to the southeast of the fault rupture, where the Space Needle swayed perceptibly. The earthquake caused rivers, lakes, and other waterways to slosh as far away as the coasts of Texas and Louisiana.
geo-quake-03-c3.claim: Next comes the Great Alaska earthquake of March 27, 1964, magnitude 9.2: the largest in US history and the second largest ever recorded with modern instruments. It swayed Seattle's Space Needle more than 1,200 miles away and sloshed waterways as far as the coasts of Texas and Louisiana.

geo-quake-03-c3.text: Brocher, T. M., Filson, J. R., Fuis, G. S., Haeussler, P. J., Holzer, T. L., Plafker, G., & Blair, J. L. (2014). The 1964 Great Alaska Earthquake and Tsunamis: A Modern Perspective and Enduring Legacies. USGS Fact Sheet 2014-3018.
geo-quake-03-c3.quote: It was so large that it caused the entire Earth to ring like a bell: vibrations that were among the first of their kind ever recorded by modern instruments.
geo-quake-03-c3.claim: It was so large that it set the whole Earth ringing like a bell.

geo-quake-03-c3.text: U.S. Geological Survey (n.d.). M 9.1 - 2004 Sumatra - Andaman Islands Earthquake: Tectonic Summary. ANSS Comprehensive Earthquake Catalog event page.
geo-quake-03-c3.quote: The devastating M 9.1 earthquake off the west coast of northern Sumatra on December 26, 2004
geo-quake-03-c3.claim: The Sumatra earthquake of December 26, 2004 stands at 9.1,

geo-quake-03-c3.text: U.S. Geological Survey (n.d.). M 9.1 - 2011 Great Tohoku Earthquake, Japan: Tectonic Summary. ANSS Comprehensive Earthquake Catalog event page.
geo-quake-03-c3.quote: The March 11, 2011, M 9.1 Tohoku earthquake, which occurred near the northeast coast of Honshu, Japan
geo-quake-03-c3.claim: and so does Japan's Tōhoku earthquake of March 11, 2011.

geo-quake-03-c3.text: U.S. Geological Survey (n.d.). M 9.1 - 2011 Great Tohoku Earthquake, Japan: Tectonic Summary. ANSS Comprehensive Earthquake Catalog event page.
geo-quake-03-c3.quote: Modeling of the rupture of this earthquake indicates that the fault moved as much as 50–60 m, and slipped over an area approximately 400 km long (along strike) by 150 km wide (in the down-dip direction).
geo-quake-03-c3.claim: Quakes this big reshape the land. The Tōhoku fault slipped as much as 50 to 60 m over an area about 400 km long and 150 km wide.

geo-quake-03-c3.text: Nishimura, T., Munekane, H., & Yarai, H. (2011). The 2011 off the Pacific coast of Tohoku Earthquake and its aftershocks observed by GEONET. Earth, Planets and Space, 63, 22.
geo-quake-03-c3.quote: The displacement was characterized by the eastward displacement and subsidence in the Pacific coastal area. The horizontal displacement exceeded 5.3 m, which is the largest ever detected by GEONET.
geo-quake-03-c3.claim: Japan's coast lurched east: on the Oshika Peninsula the ground moved more than 5.3 m, the largest shift Japan's national GPS network had ever detected.

geo-quake-03-c3.text: NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory (2011). Japan Quake May Have Shortened Earth Days, Moved Axis. JPL News, March 14, 2011.
geo-quake-03-c3.quote: His calculations indicate that by changing the distribution of Earth's mass, the Japanese earthquake should have caused Earth to rotate a bit faster, shortening the length of the day by about 1.8 microseconds
geo-quake-03-c3.claim: They even change how fast the planet turns. By shifting Earth's mass, Tōhoku should have made Earth spin a little faster, shortening each day by about 1.8 microseconds, by the calculation of Richard Gross at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory.

geo-quake-03-c3.text: NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory (2011). Japan Quake May Have Shortened Earth Days, Moved Axis. JPL News, March 14, 2011.
geo-quake-03-c3.quote: A similar calculation performed after the 2004 magnitude 9.1 Sumatran earthquake revealed it should have shortened the length of day by 6.8 microseconds and shifted Earth's figure axis by about 7 centimeters, or 2.76 inches. How an individual earthquake affects Earth's rotation depends on its size (magnitude), location and the details of how the fault slipped.
geo-quake-03-c3.claim: His estimate for Sumatra's 2004 quake was 6.8 microseconds: the effect depends on where a quake strikes and how its fault slips, not just on magnitude.

geo-quake-03-c3.text: NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory (2011). Japan Quake May Have Shortened Earth Days, Moved Axis. JPL News, March 14, 2011.
geo-quake-03-c3.quote: Over the course of a year, the length of the day increases and decreases by about a millisecond, or about 550 times larger than the change caused by the Japanese earthquake.
geo-quake-03-c3.claim: Nobody will feel it: over a year, the length of the day rises and falls by about a millisecond, some 550 times the change from the earthquake.

geo-quake-04-c1.text: U.S. Geological Survey (n.d.). Where do earthquakes occur? USGS Frequently Asked Questions.
geo-quake-04-c1.quote: The world's greatest earthquake belt, the circum-Pacific seismic belt, is found along the rim of the Pacific Ocean, where about 81 percent of our planet's largest earthquakes occur. It has earned the nickname "Ring of Fire". Why do so many earthquakes originate in this region? The belt exists along boundaries of tectonic plates, where plates of mostly oceanic crust are sinking (or subducting) beneath another plate.
geo-quake-04-c1.claim: Trace the rim of the Pacific Ocean, from Chile up to Alaska and down past Japan, and you have outlined the world's greatest earthquake belt. About 81 percent of the planet's largest earthquakes strike along this circum-Pacific belt, nicknamed the Ring of Fire, where plates of mostly ocean crust are sinking, or subducting, beneath their neighbors.

geo-quake-04-c1.text: U.S. Geological Survey (n.d.). Where do earthquakes occur? USGS Frequently Asked Questions.
geo-quake-04-c1.quote: The Alpide earthquake belt extends from Java to Sumatra through the Himalayas, the Mediterranean, and out into the Atlantic. This belt accounts for about 17 percent of the world's largest earthquakes, including some of the most destructive, such as the 2005 M7.6 shock in Pakistan that killed over 80,000 and the 2004 M9.1 Indonesia earthquake
geo-quake-04-c1.claim: The second belt, the Alpide, runs from Java and Sumatra through the Himalayas and the Mediterranean into the Atlantic and accounts for about 17 percent, including the magnitude 9.1 off Sumatra in 2004.

geo-quake-04-c1.text: Shedlock, K. M., & Pakiser, L. C. (1995). Earthquakes: Where Earthquakes Occur. USGS General Interest Publication.
geo-quake-04-c1.quote: Subduction zones are characterized by deep-ocean trenches, shallow to deep earthquakes, and mountain ranges containing active volcanoes.
geo-quake-04-c1.claim: Subduction zones bring deep-ocean trenches, earthquakes from shallow to deep, and mountain ranges with active volcanoes, which supply the fire in the name.

geo-quake-04-c1.text: U.S. Geological Survey (n.d.). M 9.1 - 2011 Great Tohoku Earthquake, Japan: Tectonic Summary. ANSS Comprehensive Earthquake Catalog event page.
geo-quake-04-c1.quote: resulted from shallow thrust faulting on the subduction zone plate boundary between the Pacific and North America plates. At the location of this earthquake, the Pacific plate moves roughly westward relative to the North America plate at a velocity of 83 mm/yr, and begins its westward descent beneath Japan at the Japan Trench
geo-quake-04-c1.claim: The giants come from one kind of fault. Where a plate dives, its top grinds beneath the plate above along a vast thrust fault called a megathrust. Off Japan the Pacific plate moves west at about 83 mm a year and starts its descent at the Japan Trench, and the 2011 Tōhoku earthquake was thrust faulting on that plate boundary.

geo-quake-04-c1.text: U.S. Geological Survey (n.d.). M 9.1 - 2004 Sumatra - Andaman Islands Earthquake: Tectonic Summary. ANSS Comprehensive Earthquake Catalog event page.
geo-quake-04-c1.quote: Since 1900, earthquakes similarly sized or larger than the December 26th earthquake have been the M 9.0 1952 Kamchatka earthquake, the M 9.5 1960 Chile earthquake, and the M 9.2 1964 Prince William Sound, Alaska, earthquake. All of these earthquakes, like the December 26th earthquake, were megathrust events, occurring where one tectonic plate subducts beneath another.
geo-quake-04-c1.claim: Before it, the largest quakes since 1900 were Kamchatka in 1952 (9.0), Chile in 1960 (9.5), Alaska in 1964 (9.2) and Sumatra in 2004, and all of them were megathrust events, where one plate subducts beneath another.

geo-quake-04-c1.text: U.S. Geological Survey (n.d.). M 9.1 - 2004 Sumatra - Andaman Islands Earthquake: Tectonic Summary. ANSS Comprehensive Earthquake Catalog event page.
geo-quake-04-c1.quote: The width of the earthquake rupture, measured perpendicular to the Sunda Trench, was about 150 km, and maximum displacement on the fault plane was upwards of 20 m.
geo-quake-04-c1.claim: Megathrusts win because moment grows with fault area, and few faults are so big. A subduction boundary can run for thousands of kilometers, and the 2004 Sumatra rupture was about 150 km wide, with slip of more than 20 m on the fault.

geo-quake-04-c2.text: U.S. Geological Survey (n.d.). M 7.5 - Northeastern Arkansas (New Madrid Seismic Zone), December 16, 1811: Impact. ANSS Comprehensive Earthquake Catalog event page, abridged from Stover & Coffman (1993), USGS Professional Paper 1527.
geo-quake-04-c2.quote: The area of strong shaking associated with these shocks is two to three times larger than that of the 1964 Alaska earthquake and 10 times larger than that of the 1906 San Francisco earthquake.
geo-quake-04-c2.claim: In the winter of 1811–12 the Mississippi valley, deep inside North America, was hit by earthquakes whose area of strong shaking was two to three times that of the 1964 Alaska earthquake and ten times that of San Francisco's in 1906.

geo-quake-04-c2.text: U.S. Geological Survey (n.d.). M 7.5 - Northeastern Arkansas (New Madrid Seismic Zone), December 16, 1811: Impact. ANSS Comprehensive Earthquake Catalog event page, abridged from Stover & Coffman (1993), USGS Professional Paper 1527.
geo-quake-04-c2.quote: The first and second principal earthquakes occurred in Arkansas about 5 hours apart on December 16, 1811 [note that the second earthquake on December 16 is now considered to be an aftershock instead of a principal earthquake] and the third and fourth [now, second and third] occurred in Missouri on January 23 and February 7, 1812.
geo-quake-04-c2.claim: There were three principal earthquakes, on December 16, 1811, January 23, 1812 and February 7, 1812.

geo-quake-04-c2.text: U.S. Geological Survey (n.d.). M 7.5 - Northeastern Arkansas (New Madrid Seismic Zone), December 16, 1811: Impact. ANSS Comprehensive Earthquake Catalog event page, abridged from Stover & Coffman (1993), USGS Professional Paper 1527.
geo-quake-04-c2.quote: Five scientific studies between 1996 and 2011 have assigned Mw magnitudes from as low as 6.8 (2011) to as high as 8.1 (1996) for this earthquake. The 2014 edition of the National Seismic Hazard Map has adopted Mw 7.5 as the best average magnitude
geo-quake-04-c2.claim: No seismographs existed, so sizes come from old accounts: studies range from 6.8 to 8.1 for the first quake, and the USGS hazard maps adopt 7.5.

geo-quake-04-c2.text: Encyclopedia of Arkansas (n.d.). New Madrid Earthquakes of 1811-1812. Central Arkansas Library System.
geo-quake-04-c2.quote: As fissures opened in the riverbed and the banks collapsed, the water was forced to run backward, or upstream, until the temporary island was washed away. Most accounts said it lasted a few minutes
geo-quake-04-c2.claim: Accounts tell of the Mississippi running backward, for a few minutes in most versions.

geo-quake-04-c2.text: U.S. Geological Survey (n.d.). M 7.5 - Northeastern Arkansas (New Madrid Seismic Zone), December 16, 1811: Impact. ANSS Comprehensive Earthquake Catalog event page, abridged from Stover & Coffman (1993), USGS Professional Paper 1527.
geo-quake-04-c2.quote: Local uplifts of the ground and water waves moving upstream gave the illusion that the river was flowing upstream.
geo-quake-04-c2.claim: The USGS catalog gives the sober reading: local uplifts of the ground and waves moving upstream gave the illusion that the river was flowing upstream.

geo-quake-04-c2.text: U.S. Geological Survey (n.d.). M 7.0 - The 1886 Charleston, South Carolina Earthquake: Impact. ANSS Comprehensive Earthquake Catalog event page, abridged from Stover & Coffman (1993), USGS Professional Paper 1527.
geo-quake-04-c2.quote: It struck about 9:51 P.M. local time on August 31, and damaged or destroyed many buildings in the old city of Charleston and killed 60 people. Hardly a structure there was undamaged, and only a few escaped serious damage.
geo-quake-04-c2.claim: On August 31, 1886, an earthquake wrecked Charleston, South Carolina, and killed 60 people. Hardly a building in the city escaped damage.

geo-quake-04-c2.text: Shedlock, K. M., & Pakiser, L. C. (1995). Earthquakes: Where Earthquakes Occur. USGS General Interest Publication.
geo-quake-04-c2.quote: Less than 10 percent of all earthquakes occur within plate interiors. As plates continue to move and plate boundaries change over geologic time, weakened boundary regions become part of the interiors of the plates. These zones of weakness within the continents can cause earthquakes in response to stresses that originate at the edges of the plate or in the deeper crust. The New Madrid earthquakes of 1811-1812 and the 1886 Charleston earthquake occurred within the North American plate.
geo-quake-04-c2.claim: Both struck inside the North American plate, far from its edges, and quakes like that are uncommon: fewer than 10 percent of all earthquakes occur within plate interiors. Old, weakened zones inside a continent can still fail under stresses that come from the plate's edges or the deeper crust.

geo-quake-04-c2.text: U.S. Geological Survey (n.d.). M 5.8 - Central Virginia, August 23, 2011: Tectonic Summary. ANSS Comprehensive Earthquake Catalog event page.
geo-quake-04-c2.quote: Earthquakes in the central and eastern U.S., although less frequent than in the western U.S., are typically felt over a much broader region. East of the Rockies, an earthquake can be felt over an area as much as ten times larger than a similar magnitude earthquake on the west coast.
geo-quake-04-c2.claim: Eastern quakes also reach farther. East of the Rockies, an earthquake can be felt over an area as much as ten times larger than one of similar magnitude on the West Coast.

geo-quake-04-c2.text: Pappas, S. (2011). Why Virginia Quake Shook Entire Coast. Live Science, August 23, 2011.
geo-quake-04-c2.quote: "The crust is different in the east than in the west," United States Geological Survey (USGS) earthquake geologist David Schwartz told LiveScience. "It's older and colder and denser, and as a result, seismic waves travel much farther in the east than in the west."
geo-quake-04-c2.claim: When a magnitude 5.8 quake in Virginia rattled the East Coast in 2011, USGS geologist David Schwartz explained why: the eastern crust is older, colder and denser, so seismic waves travel much farther there.

geo-quake-04-c3.text: Walter, J. I., Ogwari, P., Thiel, A., Ferrer, F., Woelfel, I., Chang, J. C., Darold, A. P., & Holland, A. A. (2020). The Oklahoma Geological Survey Statewide Seismic Network. Seismological Research Letters, 91(2A), 611-621 (abstract via Sandia National Laboratories).
geo-quake-04-c3.quote: In Oklahoma, before 2009, background seismicity rates were about 2 M 3.0+ earthquakes per year, which increased to 579 and 903 M 3.0+ earthquakes in 2014 and 2015, respectively. After seismicity peaked, the rate fell to 624, 304, and 194 M 3.0+ earthquakes in 2016, 2017, and 2018, respectively.
geo-quake-04-c3.claim: By the Oklahoma Geological Survey's count, the state had about 2 earthquakes of magnitude 3 or more a year before 2009. In 2014 it had 579, and in 2015, 903. Then the count fell: 624 in 2016, 304 in 2017 and 194 in 2018.

geo-quake-04-c3.text: U.S. Geological Survey (n.d.). M 5.8 - 14 km NW of Pawnee, Oklahoma: Impact. ANSS Comprehensive Earthquake Catalog event page.
geo-quake-04-c3.quote: As of July 2026 this is the largest earthquake located within the State of Oklahoma.
geo-quake-04-c3.claim: The strongest, a magnitude 5.8 near Pawnee in September 2016, remains the largest earthquake ever located in Oklahoma.

geo-quake-04-c3.text: Walsh, F. R., III, & Zoback, M. D. (2015). Oklahoma's recent earthquakes and saltwater disposal. Science Advances, 1(5), e1500195.
geo-quake-04-c3.quote: In the areas of seismic activity, the saltwater disposal principally comes from “produced” water, saline pore water that is coproduced with oil and then injected into deeper sedimentary formations.
geo-quake-04-c3.claim: The main culprit was not fracking itself but wastewater. In the active areas, most of the fluid pumped into deep disposal wells was salty water that comes up with the oil, not water used to fracture the rock.

geo-quake-04-c3.text: Walsh, F. R., III, & Zoback, M. D. (2015). Oklahoma's recent earthquakes and saltwater disposal. Science Advances, 1(5), e1500195.
geo-quake-04-c3.quote: Simply put, increased fluid pressure decreases the effective normal stress on a fault. The effective normal stress resists fault slip by acting perpendicular to the fault, in a sense clamping the fault. Because an increase in pore pressure reduces the effective normal stress, it acts to unclamp a fault, potentially triggering the release of accumulated strain energy on a preexisting fault that is already close to failure
geo-quake-04-c3.claim: Raising the fluid pressure deep underground weakens the clamping force that holds a fault shut, so a fault already close to failure can slip.

geo-quake-04-c3.text: Langenbruch, C., & Zoback, M. D. (2016). How will induced seismicity in Oklahoma respond to decreased saltwater injection rates? Science Advances, 2(11), e1601542.
geo-quake-04-c3.quote: in February and March 2016, Oklahoma regulators called for a 40% reduction in the injection volume for 2016 compared to the volume injected in 2014
geo-quake-04-c3.claim: In early 2016 the state's regulators called for a 40 percent cut in injection volume in the most active areas.

geo-quake-04-c3.text: Muntendam-Bos, A. G., & Grobbe, N. (2022). Data-driven spatiotemporal assessment of the event-size distribution of the Groningen extraction-induced seismicity catalogue. Scientific Reports, 12, 10119.
geo-quake-04-c3.quote: The Groningen gas field, located in the north-east of the Netherlands, is the largest gas field in Europe and the tenth largest in the world (Fig. 1). In recent years, it was one of the most studied fields in terms of induced seismicity (e.g.22–27). At the same time, a lot of open questions and concerns remain. The field has been associated with induced seismicity since December 5, 1991
geo-quake-04-c3.claim: Taking fluid out can do it too. Groningen, in the northeastern Netherlands, is the largest gas field in Europe, and its gas extraction has set off earthquakes since 1991.

geo-quake-04-c3.text: Nederlandse Aardolie Maatschappij (n.d.). English information. NAM.
geo-quake-04-c3.quote: On August 16, 2012, an earthquake with a magnitude of 3.6 on the Richter scale occurred near Huizinge. This earthquake was felt more strongly by residents than previous seismic activity.
geo-quake-04-c3.claim: The strongest, magnitude 3.6 near Huizinge on August 16, 2012, was felt more strongly than anything before it.

geo-quake-04-c3.text: Wright, B. (2024). Groningen Gas Field To Shut Down for Good. Journal of Petroleum Technology (Society of Petroleum Engineers), April 21, 2024.
geo-quake-04-c3.quote: Dutch leaders have voted to halt all future production from the large gas field due to seismic activity linked to extraction operations.
geo-quake-04-c3.claim: In 2024 Dutch leaders voted to halt all future production from the field because of the quakes.
